implementation_notes: ThreadLocal<T> is the CLR's general-purpose realization: the instance is the access point, a valueFactory runs once per thread on first access, Value and IsValueCreated are specific to the calling thread, and every member except Dispose() is thread-safe. The classic key/collection/proxy structure is replaced by the CLR's thread-static storage block maintained by the instance; the price is that the values held for other threads are only released by Dispose() (or when those threads end), so a long-lived static ThreadLocal<T> in a server must be disposed deliberately. Use AsyncLocal<T> instead whenever the ambient data has to follow an asynchronous control flow rather than a thread.
pitfalls: Values for other threads are retained until Dispose() or until those threads die: a static ThreadLocal<T> in an application with many short-lived threads leaks unless it is disposed.
ThreadLocal<T> does not follow await: the continuation may run on a different pooled thread, so request state stored here is lost or, worse, read from another request.
trackAllValues/Values exists for diagnostics and keeps strong references to every thread's value, multiplying the retention it is meant to help diagnose.

variants.name: [ThreadStatic] per-thread static field
variants.implementation_notes: For a field of a known type, [ThreadStatic] makes the static field itself per-thread: each executing thread has its own instance and reads and writes it independently, which the .NET documentation recommends as the fastest mechanism when the set of thread-relative fields is known at compile time. What replaces the classic structure is the field plus the CLR's per-thread static block - no key, no collection, no factory. Two rules come with it: the field must be static, and it must not be initialised inline, because the static constructor runs on one thread only, so every other thread sees the default value.
variants.code_sketch:
[ThreadStatic] static RequestContext? _current;   // no initialiser: other threads see null

static RequestContext Current =>
    _current ??= RequestContext.Create();          // lazy per thread, no lock needed
pitfalls: An inline initialiser (or a static constructor assignment) runs once on the first thread only; every other thread then reads null/default - initialise lazily instead.
[ThreadStatic] is not reset when a pooled thread is reused, so a work item inherits the previous item's value unless the code clears it.
It does not flow across await and is not inherited by new threads; for async code use AsyncLocal<T> and for child-thread propagation pass the value explicitly.
